vignette:
Marcus

Marcus sits in the leather chair across from the therapist's desk with his shoulders squared, the posture of someone accustomed to commanding attention. At forty-nine, he still carries the bearing of the soldier he was thirty years ago—spine straight, jaw set, eyes that scan the room before settling. His wedding band catches the light as he adjusts his tie, a nervous gesture that contradicts his otherwise composed presentation.

He was nineteen when he deployed to the Balkans in 1994. Marcus had joined the military to escape a small town and prove something to himself. What he found instead was chaos—the kind that doesn't announce itself but arrives in fragments. The mortar attack happened on a Tuesday. He remembers this clearly, though he wishes he didn't. Twelve soldiers in his unit. Three didn't leave the valley. Marcus carried one of them.

For years afterward, he functioned. He left the service, went to college, built a career in municipal government. He married Sarah, a woman who knew something was different about him but loved him anyway. They have two adult children. On the surface, Marcus has done everything right. He was elected to city council six years ago, running on a platform of infrastructure and community development. He's respected, effective, known for his level-headedness in contentious meetings.

But the nights have become impossible. Marcus lies awake beside Sarah, his mind replaying moments he's tried to bury. The sound of the explosion—not the explosion itself, but the silence after it, the ringing that lasted for days. He jolts awake sometimes, his body convinced it's happening again, convinced he's still twenty-two and covered in dust that won't come clean. Sarah has learned not to reach for him when he wakes. Once, he nearly struck her in his confusion between dream and reality.

During the day, he's managed, mostly. But three months ago, a construction accident near City Hall sent a loud crash through the building. Marcus found himself under his desk, breathing in short gasps, unable to explain to the concerned staff members why he was there. He told them it was dizziness. He told Sarah it was nothing. It wasn't nothing.

The hypervigilance has worsened. In council meetings, he's acutely aware of exits, of who sits near him, of sounds outside the chamber. When a colleague raised their voice during a debate last week, Marcus's hand instinctively moved toward where a weapon would have been. He's aware of how absurd this is—a middle-aged city councilman in a government building—and yet his body doesn't care about context. His nervous system is still in the Balkans, still waiting for the next attack.

He's started avoiding public events, which is complicated for someone in his position. Crowds feel dangerous. He's made excuses about being busy, about needing to focus on work. Sarah knows better. She's suggested he talk to someone, and he's resisted for months. The idea of speaking about what happened feels like a betrayal somehow—like weakness, like he's finally admitting that the explosion didn't just happen thirty years ago; it's still happening, still shaping every decision, every moment.

Marcus is here now because Sarah gave him an ultimatum delivered with love: get help or watch her step back from their marriage. He loves her more than he loves his pride. So he sits in this chair, hands clasped, trying to find words for things he's spent three decades not saying, wondering if there's any way back from a place he never truly left.
